stem: A 72-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic for a routine follow-up visit. She has no dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, flank pain, fever, or chills. Her diabetes is well-managed with metformin and glipizide, and her most recent hemoglobin A1c is 7.2%. On physical examination, she is afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal examination is soft, non-tender, and without costovertebral angle tenderness. Routine urinalysis obtained as part of an outpatient order demonstrates: 2+ leukocyte esterase, negative nitrites, and 15 to 20 WBCs per high-power field. A clean-catch midstream urine culture subsequently grows > 100,000 colony-forming units/mL of pan-susceptible Escherichia coli. The patient remains completely asymptomatic and feels well. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Prescribe a 7-day course of oral ciprofloxacin to eradicate bacteriuria and prevent pyelonephritis
options.explanation: Fluoroquinolones in asymptomatic bacteriuria promote resistance, tendonitis, and C. difficile without preventing pyelonephritis in diabetic elderly patients.

options.text: No antimicrobial therapy and reassurance, as treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is not indicated
options.explanation: This patient has ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA (ASB), defined as isolation of >= 10^5 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL of a single bacterial strain in a voided clean-catch urine sample from an individual without any signs or symptoms of a urinary tract infection (no dysuria, frequency, urgency, fever, or flank pain). The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines firmly dictate that ASB SHOULD NOT BE SCREENED FOR OR TREATED in the vast majority of clinical populations—including elderly individuals, diabetic patients, postmenopausal women, institutionalized nursing home residents, patients with indwelling bladder catheters, or spinal cord injury patients. Clinical trials have conclusively shown that treating ASB in these cohorts confers zero clinical benefit (it does not reduce future UTI episodes, sepsis, or mortality) and directly causes harm, including adverse drug reactions, Clostridioides difficile colitis, and the emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens. There are only TWO ABSOLUTE INDICATIONS to screen and treat ASB: (1) PREGNANT WOMEN (to prevent acute pyelonephritis, preterm labor, and low birth weight); and (2) PATIENTS UNDERGOING UROLOGIC PROCEDURES involving mucosal bleeding (such as transurethral resection of the prostate).

options.text: Prescribe a 5-day course of oral nitrofurantoin to sterilize the urinary tract
options.explanation: Even narrow-spectrum antibiotics like nitrofurantoin provide no survival or symptomatic benefit in ASB and lead to recurrent colonization with resistant flora.

options.text: Order a non-contrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis to evaluate for emphysematous cystitis
options.explanation: Emphysematous cystitis presents with severe sepsis, abdominal pain, and pneumaturia in uncontrolled diabetics; asymptomatic bacteriuria requires no imaging.

options.text: Repeat the urine culture in 2 weeks and treat if the same bacterial organism persists
options.explanation: Serial surveillance cultures and treating persistent asymptomatic colonization are explicitly discouraged by IDSA antimicrobial stewardship guidelines.

subject: Medicine
topic: Primary Aldosteronism Diagnostic Algorithm
stem: A 44-year-old man presents to the clinic for follow-up of persistent hypertension. Despite adherence to a three-drug antihypertensive regimen consisting of lisinopril 40 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, and chlorthalidone 25 mg daily, his blood pressure today is 168/102 mm Hg. He complains of intermittent muscle weakness and fatigue. On physical examination, his BMI is 27 kg/m², heart rate is 74/min, and cardiopulmonary examination is normal. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: serum sodium 144 mEq/L, serum potassium 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.5-5.0 mEq/L), serum bicarbonate 31 mEq/L, and serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. He is screened for secondary hypertension: plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) is 32 ng/dL (normal < 15 ng/dL), and plasma renin activity (PRA) is suppressed at 0.4 ng/mL/hr (PAC/PRA ratio = 80). Confirmatory intravenous saline suppression testing confirms autonomous hyperaldosteronism. An unenhanced thin-slice CT scan of the adrenal glands demonstrates a well-circumscribed, 1.2-cm hypodense nodule in the left adrenal gland; the right adrenal gland appears normal. The patient wishes to pursue curative surgical resection. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before proceeding to surgery?

options.text: Immediate left laparoscopic adrenalectomy based on the visible CT nodule
options.explanation: Proceeding directly to surgery without adrenal venous sampling leads to wrong-gland removal or inappropriate adrenalectomy in patients with bilateral hyperplasia who have an incidental non-functioning nodule.

options.text: Initiation of high-dose oral spironolactone monotherapy and cancellation of surgical workup
options.explanation: In a 44-year-old patient who desires surgical cure, completing the lateralization workup with AVS is indicated because unilateral adenomas can be completely cured surgically.

options.text: Adrenal venous sampling (AVS) to differentiate unilateral from bilateral aldosterone hypersecretion
options.explanation: This patient presents with classic PRIMARY ALDOSTERONISM (Conn syndrome) characterized by treatment-resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and a markedly elevated plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (PAC/PRA = 80). Autonomous production was confirmed via failure to suppress aldosterone after saline infusion. The two primary etiologies of primary aldosteronism are: (1) Unilateral aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma (~50-60% of cases), which is curable with laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy; and (2) Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (~40-50% of cases), which must be managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone or eplerenone). CRITICAL MANAGEMENT STEP: Adrenal CT scanning has notoriously poor diagnostic accuracy for lateralization because non-functioning incidental adrenal adenomas ("incidentalomas") are highly prevalent in patients > 40 years old, and microadenomas or bilateral hyperplasia may appear normal on CT. Therefore, guidelines from the Endocrine Society mandate ADRENAL VENOUS SAMPLING (AVS) in all surgical candidates to measure aldosterone levels directly from both adrenal veins and the IVC. If AVS confirms unilateral hypersecretion matching the CT nodule, unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy provides cure; if bilateral hypersecretion is demonstrated, surgery is avoided in favor of spironolactone.

options.text: Twenty-four-hour urinary metanephrines and normetanephrines quantification
options.explanation: Urinary metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma (headache, sweating, tachycardia, episodic hypertension); autonomous aldosterone with suppressed renin confirms primary aldosteronism.

options.text: Renal artery duplex ultrasonography to evaluate for renal artery stenosis
options.explanation: Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism with HIGH plasma renin activity, whereas this patient has autonomous aldosterone with a SUPPRESSED plasma renin activity (0.4 ng/mL/hr).

SCREENING: Morning PLASMA ALDOSTERONE CONCENTRATION TO PLASMA RENIN ACTIVITY RATIO (PAC/PRA ratio > 20 with PAC > 15 ng/dL); 2. CONFIRMATORY TEST: Saline infusion test or oral sodium loading (fails to suppress aldosterone); 3. ADRENAL CT SCAN to evaluate anatomy; 4. ADRENAL VENOUS SAMPLING (AVS) is MANDATORY to differentiate UNILATERAL ADENOMA (treated with LAPAROSCOPIC ADRENALECTOMY) from BILATERAL HYPERPLASIA (treated medically with SPIRONOLACTONE/EPLERENONE).

subject: Medicine
topic: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Diagnostic Testing and Splinting
stem: A 41-year-old administrative assistant presents to the clinic reporting a 4-month history of intermittent tingling, burning, and numbness affecting her right hand. The symptoms characteristically awaken her from sleep at night, forcing her to shake her hand vigorously to obtain relief ("flick sign"). She notes that the numbness is localized to her thumb, index finger, middle finger, and the thumb-side of her ring finger. Over the past month, she has dropped coffee mugs on two occasions due to clumsiness. On physical examination, there is normal sensation over the right thenar eminence, but sensation to two-point discrimination is impaired over the palmar aspect of the index and middle fingertips. Tapping lightly over the volar aspect of the right wrist elicits sharp paresthesias radiating into the thumb and index finger (positive Tinel sign). Holding both wrists in complete unforced flexion for 60 seconds reproduces intense numbness in the median nerve distribution (positive Phalen test). Manual muscle testing reveals normal 5/5 abductor pollicis brevis strength, and there is no visible thenar muscle atrophy. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial conservative management for this patient?

options.text: Immediate open surgical decompression with transverse carpal ligament division
options.explanation: Surgical carpal tunnel release is indicated for severe refractory CTS that fails conservative therapy or when electrodiagnostic studies show severe axonal loss or visible thenar muscle atrophy.

options.text: Oral high-dose prednisone for 4 weeks followed by physical therapy exercises
options.explanation: Systemic oral corticosteroids carry significant systemic adverse effects and are far less effective and durable than local conservative neutral wrist splinting.

options.text: Continuous long-term wearing of an elastic wrist bandage while typing at work
options.explanation: Elastic compression bandages compress the carpal tunnel further and do not maintain the rigid neutral wrist posture necessary to alleviate median nerve compression.

options.text: Prescription of a rigid wrist splint maintained in a neutral position to be worn every night during sleep
options.explanation: This patient presents with classic, moderate CARPAL TUNNEL SYNDROME (CTS), the most common entrapment neuropathy of the upper extremity. CTS results from compression and ischemia of the median nerve as it courses beneath the rigid transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum) within the carpal tunnel. Hallmark clinical features include: (1) Paresthesias, burning, and pain localized to the median nerve sensory territory (thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger); (2) Nocturnal symptom exacerbation that awakens the patient, relieved by vigorous hand shaking ("flick sign"); (3) Sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence itself, because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve branches proximal to the carpal tunnel and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum; and (4) Positive provocative tests (Phalen maneuver and Tinel sign). The gold-standard first-line conservative intervention is NOCTURNAL NEUTRAL WRIST SPLINTING. During sleep, individuals naturally assume positions of wrist flexion or extreme extension, which dramatically elevates intracarpal canal pressure and compresses the median nerve. Immobilizing the wrist in a neutral (0-degree) position maximizes the cross-sectional area of the carpal tunnel, lowering tissue pressure and providing significant symptom relief.

options.text: Performance of magnetic resonance neurography of the cervical spine and brachial plexus
options.explanation: Cervical spine imaging is unnecessary when the physical examination, nocturnal awakenings, positive Phalen, and Tinel signs clearly localize the pathology to the carpal tunnel.

Symptoms worse at night. Positive Phalen test (flexion of wrists reproduces numbness) and Tinel sign. Thenar atrophy is a late finding. - FIRST-LINE INITIAL THERAPY: NOCTURNAL WRIST SPLINTING IN A NEUTRAL POSITION (relieves elevated intracarpal canal pressures during sleep). Second-line: Local corticosteroid injection; Refractory/severe: Surgical transverse carpal ligament release.

subject: Medicine
topic: GERD with Alarm Symptoms Diagnostic Approach
stem: A 59-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 5-month history of worsening heartburn and retrosternal burning pain after meals. Over the past 6 weeks, he has developed progressive difficulty swallowing solid foods, such as bread and steak, describing a sensation of food "getting stuck" in the lower chest that requires him to drink large amounts of water to wash it down. He has no difficulty swallowing liquids. Over the last 2 months, he has had an unintended weight loss of 14 lbs and poor appetite. His medical history includes hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide and a 30-pack-year smoking history. On physical examination, the patient appears thin. His blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg, heart rate is 76/min, and BMI is 21 kg/m². Abdominal examination is soft and non-tender without palpable masses or organomegaly; there is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Complete blood count demonstrates: hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 74 fL (microcytic anemia), and stool guaiac test is positive for occult blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the clinical management of this patient?

options.text: Prescribe twice-daily high-dose oral omeprazole and re-evaluate symptoms in 8 weeks
options.explanation: Escalating empiric acid suppression in the presence of dysphagia, weight loss, and anemia causes fatal diagnostic delays in resectable esophageal adenocarcinoma.

options.text: Perform a 24-hour ambulatory esophageal pH-impedance monitoring study
options.explanation: Esophageal pH monitoring evaluates refractory atypical reflux or confirms GERD prior to anti-reflux surgery in patients with normal endoscopy; it does not evaluate mechanical dysphagia or cancer.

options.text: Order high-resolution esophageal manometry to assess for achalasia
options.explanation: Manometry is indicated for motor dysmotility (dysphagia to both solids and liquids simultaneously); progressive dysphagia to solids alone in an older smoker requires endoscopy to exclude cancer.

options.text: Initiate oral sucralfate suspension and schedule a repeat clinic visit in 3 months
options.explanation: Sucralfate is a mucosal coating agent that has zero efficacy in evaluating or treating malignant mechanical esophageal obstruction.

options.text: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) with mucosal biopsies
options.explanation: This 59-year-old man presents with typical gastroesophageal reflux symptoms complicated by multiple major ALARM FEATURES: (1) Progressive mechanical dysphagia (difficulty swallowing solids); (2) Significant unintended weight loss (14 lbs); (3) Age > 50 years; and (4) New microcytic iron-deficiency anemia with occult gastrointestinal blood loss. While uncomplicated GERD is managed empirically with an 8-week course of once-daily proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), the presence of ANY alarm feature is an absolute indication for IMMEDIATE UPPER ENDOSCOPY (ESOPHAGOGASTRODUODENOSCOPY - EGD) WITH MUCOSAL BIOPSIES. The primary concern is ESOPHAGEAL ADENOCARCINOMA (which typically arises from pre-existing Barrett esophagus in the distal third of the esophagus, especially in older male smokers with chronic GERD) or an advanced peptic esophageal stricture. Endoscopy allows direct visualization of the mucosal architecture, identification of luminal obstruction, and acquisition of targeted histological tissue biopsies for definitive pathological diagnosis. Empiric medical therapy or barium swallow must not delay diagnostic endoscopy.
